etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From French idéal, from Late Latin ideālis (“existing in idea”), by surface analysis, idea +‎ -al, from Latin idea (“idea”); see idea.
In mathematics, the noun ring theory sense was first introduced by German mathematician Richard Dedekind in his 1871 edition of a text on number theory. The concept was quickly expanded to ring theory and later generalised to order theory. The set theory and Lie theory senses can be regarded as applications of the order theory sense.

definitions.definition: Pertaining to ideas, or to a given idea.
Existing only in the mind; conceptual, imaginary.

quote.citation: 1796, Matthew Lewis, The Monk, Folio Society, published 1985, page 256:
quote.text: The idea of ghosts is ridiculous in the extreme; and if you continue to be swayed by ideal terrors —

quote.citation: 1816 June – 1817 April/May (date written), [Mary Shelley], “Chapter 4”, in Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus. […], volume (please specify |volume=I to III), London:  […]  [Macdonald and Son] for Lackington, Hughes, Harding, Mavor, & Jones, published 1 January 1818, →OCLC:
quote.text: Life and death appeared to me ideal bounds, which I should first break through, and pour a torrent of light into our dark world.

quote.citation: 1836 March – 1837 October, Charles Dickens, “(please specify the chapter name)”, in The Posthumous Papers of the Pickwick Club, London: Chapman and Hall, […], published 1837, →OCLC:
quote.text: At first, he began to doubt the reality of his adventures, but the acute pain in his shoulders when he attempted to rise, assured him that the kicking of the goblins was certainly not ideal.

quote.citation: 1751 April 13, Samuel Johnson, The Rambler, Number 112, reprinted in 1825, The Works of Samuel Johnson, LL. D., Volume 1, Jones & Company, page 194,
quote.text: There will always be a wide interval between practical and ideal excellence; […] .

definitions.definition: Teaching or relating to the doctrine of idealism.
(mathematics) Not actually present, but considered as present when limits at infinity are included.
A thing which exists in the mind but not in reality; in ontological terms, a thing which has essence but not existence.
A perfect standard of beauty, intellect etc., or a standard of excellence to aim at.

quote.citation: 1945 April 16, Harry S. Truman, 9:21 from the start, in MP72-20 President Roosevelt’s Funeral and Procession; Truman – New President of U.S.‎[3], Harry S. Truman Presidential Library and Museum, National Archives Identifier: 595162:
quote.text: With great humility, I call upon all Americans to help me keep our nation united in defense of those ideals which have been so eloquently proclaimed by Franklin Roosevelt. I want in turn to assure my fellow Americans and all of those who love peace and liberty throughout the world that I will support and defend those ideals with all my strength and all my heart.

definitions.definition: (algebra, ring theory) A two-sided ideal; a subset of a ring which is closed under both left and right multiplication by elements of the ring.

quote.citation: 2004, K. R. Goodearl, R. B. Warfield, Jr., An Introduction to Noncommutative Noetherian Rings, 2nd edition, Cambridge University Press, page 47:
quote.text: In trying to understand the ideal theory of a commutative ring, one quickly sees that it is important to first understand the prime ideals.

quote.citation: 2009, John J. Watkins, Topics in Commutative Ring Theory, Princeton University Press, page 45:
quote.text: If an ideal I of a ring contains the multiplicative identity 1, then we have seen that I must be the entire ring.

quote.citation: 2010, W. D. Burgess, A. Lashgari, A. Mojiri, “Elements of Minimal Prime Ideals in General Rings”, in Sergio R. López-Permouth, Dinh Van Huynh, editors, Advances in Ring Theory, Springer (Birkhäuser), page 69:
quote.text: However, every R has a minimal prime ideal consisting of left zero-divisors and one of right zero-divisors.

definitions.definition: (algebra, order theory, lattice theory) A non-empty lower set (of a partially ordered set) which is closed under binary suprema (a.k.a. joins).[1]

quote.citation: 1992, Unnamed translator, T. S. Fofanova, General Theory of Lattices, in Ordered Sets and Lattices II, American Mathematical Society, page 119,
quote.text: An ideal A of L is called complete if it contains all least upper bounds of its subsets that exist in L. Bishop and Schreiner [80] studied conditions under which joins of ideals in the lattices of all ideals and of all complete ideals coincide.

quote.citation: 2011, George Grätzer, Lattice Theory: Foundation‎[4], Springer (Birkhäuser), page 125:
quote.text: 1.35 Find a distributive lattice L with no minimal and no maximal prime ideals.

quote.citation: 2015, Vijay K. Garg, Introduction to Lattice Theory with Computer Science Applications, Wiley, page 186:
quote.text: Definition 15.11 (Width Ideal) An ideal Q of a poset P = (X,≤) is a width ideal if maximal(Q) is a width antichain.

definitions.definition: (algebra, Lie theory) A Lie subalgebra (subspace that is closed under the Lie bracket) 𝖍 of a given Lie algebra 𝖌 such that the Lie bracket [𝖌,𝖍] is a subset of 𝖍.

definitions.definition: (algebra) A subsemigroup with the property that if any semigroup element outside of it is added to any one of its members, the result must lie outside of it.[2]
